title: AI Won't Replace Good Engineers ( for now ). But Good Engineers Will Use AI.
excerpt: AI is changing software engineering at a remarkable pace. The opportunity isn't to choose between AI and engineers, but to combine the two: let AI handle more of the work while experienced engineers provide the context, judgement and healthy scepticism needed to make sure the result is actually good.
content:
It's getting hard to have a conversation about software engineering without AI being somewhere in the background. The technology is moving so quickly that even people in the industry struggle to keep up. A tool that seemed revolutionary six months ago can already feel like yesterday's news, while something that sounded impossible a year ago is now being demonstrated in everyday development workflows.

As a software engineer, I find that both exciting and slightly unsettling.

AI can now write surprisingly good code. It can explain unfamiliar codebases, generate tests, investigate errors, suggest architectural approaches and produce working implementations from fairly simple descriptions. Something that might once have taken an hour of searching, experimenting and typing can become a conversation that takes a few minutes.

Which raises an obvious question: if AI can do so much of the work, what exactly is the software engineer supposed to do?

I don't think the answer is to resist AI, and I don't think it's to hand everything over to it either. The most interesting possibility sits between those extremes: a very capable AI working alongside a competent engineer who understands enough to challenge it. I'm much less interested in an AI that replaces the engineer than in what happens when you give a good engineer an incredibly powerful assistant.

## The uncomfortable truth about AI-generated code

One of the most impressive things about modern AI coding tools is also one of their biggest weaknesses: they're very good at producing something that looks right.

That sounds like an odd criticism, since good-looking code is what we want. The problem is that looking right and being right are very different things.

AI can produce a beautifully structured function with sensible variable names, appropriate patterns and a completely convincing explanation of why it works, complete with examples. You read it and think, *"That makes perfect sense."* Then you discover it has made a fundamental assumption about your application that simply isn't true. Perhaps it misunderstood how your data is structured, or used an API incorrectly. Perhaps it missed an edge case or introduced a subtle security problem. Or perhaps it solved the problem you described instead of the one you actually needed solving.

The really dangerous mistakes often aren't the ones that crash the application, because those are usually easy to find. The hard ones are solutions that work most of the time while doing the wrong thing in one particular situation.

That's why I think the ability to question AI is going to become one of the most important skills a software engineer can have. You need to be able to look at an answer and think, *"Hang on. Why has it done that?"* You need enough knowledge to challenge its assumptions, enough experience to recognise when something doesn't feel right, and enough confidence to ignore the answer entirely when necessary.

That's what I mean when I talk about being able to call bullshit on AI. And I think it will matter more as AI gets better.

## The better AI gets, the more important judgement becomes

It might seem counterintuitive, but I don't think more capable AI makes engineering knowledge less valuable. If anything, it puts a higher premium on good judgement.

Today you might ask an AI tool for five possible solutions to a technical problem. In future it might give you fifty, or five hundred, exploring an enormous number of approaches in the time it would take a human to properly investigate one. That's incredibly powerful, but it doesn't remove the decision.

Somebody still needs to understand the actual problem: the constraints of the system, the needs of the users, the implications of the architecture and the consequences of getting it wrong. AI can give you more options. It doesn't necessarily tell you which problem is worth solving.

I think one change AI will bring is that we'll spend less time manually producing every piece of code and more time deciding what should be built, evaluating what's been produced and judging whether it's the right solution. That's still engineering. The tools are just more powerful.

## Don't confuse writing code with understanding software

There's another reason I'm cautious about the idea of AI taking over large parts of software development. Writing code has never been the only difficult bit. The hard part is understanding what the software needs to do and why.

It's understanding the strange business rule that exists because of a decision made seven years ago. It's knowing that a particular database table looks redundant but can't be removed because another system depends on it, or why a seemingly sensible change would cause problems for a particular customer, or which parts of the system are fragile and which can safely be changed.

AI can help you discover some of this, but it can't automatically know all of it. A codebase is the accumulated history of decisions, compromises, requirements and mistakes made by everyone who has worked on it.

So I'd be very uncomfortable letting an AI make significant architectural decisions on its own just because it can generate a convincing proposal. By all means ask it for one, or five. Ask it to criticise your existing architecture, or what it would change if it were starting again. Those are useful exercises. But I still want an engineer who understands the system making the decision.

## AI should make you more capable

There's another trap that's easy to fall into. If AI gets good enough to do something for you, it's tempting to stop learning how to do it yourself.

At first that doesn't seem like a problem. Why spend two hours learning something when AI can give you the answer in thirty seconds? Sometimes you shouldn't. If I'm doing something repetitive that I've done a hundred times, I'd much rather have AI generate the first version and spend my time reviewing it.

But using AI to save time is different from using it to avoid understanding something. If AI always writes your SQL, do you still understand what the query is doing? If it writes a complicated piece of JavaScript, could you debug it when something goes wrong? If it proposes an architecture, can you explain the trade-offs? If its solution fails in production, could you work out why?

Those questions matter because engineers remain responsible for the software they produce. Nobody in production gets to blame the AI that wrote the code. The engineer still owns the decision.

## There's a less exciting side to AI-assisted development

Most conversations about AI in software engineering focus on productivity. How much faster can we write code? How many developers can we replace? How much can an agent do without human intervention?

A less exciting but potentially more important question is what we're actually allowed to give these systems access to.

A real-world codebase can hold a lot of sensitive material: customer data, proprietary algorithms, internal business logic, credentials, security-sensitive configuration, commercially confidential information, or code covered by third-party licences. Just because an AI coding tool *can* read something doesn't mean it *should*.

This is where the conversation moves beyond engineering into security, privacy, legal and compliance. On a personal project you might have a lot of freedom in how you use AI. On a commercial application, especially in a regulated industry, things can be very different. Your organisation may have rules about which AI tools you can use, what information you can submit to them, whether source code can be shared, how data is retained, and what human review is required before AI-generated code reaches production.

Those rules aren't just obstacles from people who don't understand technology. They exist because software has consequences. A developer accidentally sending customer information to an external service can turn into a security incident, a privacy issue, a contractual problem or a regulatory matter.

So one of the most important skills for an AI-enabled engineer may be knowing where the boundaries are. Before giving an AI tool access to your entire repository, you need to understand what you're agreeing to, what information is being processed and whether you're allowed to do it. The technology is moving quickly, but the normal responsibilities around security, privacy and compliance haven't gone anywhere.

## AI can make bad engineering incredibly efficient

There's an irony here too. AI can make you faster, but faster isn't automatically better.

Take an engineer who normally writes 100 lines of code in an afternoon and give them a tool that generates 1,000 in the same time. You've dramatically increased their output, and you've also increased the amount of code that has to be understood, reviewed, tested and maintained. AI can make good engineering faster, and it can make bad engineering faster too.

That's why I think code review, testing, version control, CI/CD, security testing and monitoring become more important in an AI-driven environment. If we're producing software faster, we need confidence that what we're producing is good.

The bottleneck may simply move. Writing the code used to take most of the time and reviewing it was relatively quick. With AI that balance could reverse: generating an implementation takes seconds, and the real work becomes deciding whether that implementation should exist at all. That feels like a significant change in the engineer's role.

## So how should we actually use AI?

I don't think there's a single correct AI workflow for software engineers. The technology is changing too quickly for anyone to claim they've found the definitive way of working.

For me, though, the principle is fairly simple: use AI aggressively where the risk is low and cautiously where the consequences are high.

AI is fantastic for helping me understand an unfamiliar piece of code. I'll happily use it for a starting point on repetitive implementation, to challenge an approach I've come up with, or to generate test cases, documentation, examples and potential edge cases. If I'm stuck, I'll explain the problem to an AI and see what it comes up with. Sometimes the answer is useless and sometimes it points me towards something I hadn't considered. I don't need it to be right every time. Another useful perspective is worth the small effort involved.

I become much more cautious when AI starts making decisions with significant consequences:

- security-sensitive changes
- critical business logic
- major architectural decisions
- production deployments
- anything involving sensitive customer information

AI doesn't have to stay away from those areas entirely, but the level of human oversight needs to go up significantly. The more expensive the mistake, the less comfortable I am simply trusting the output.

## The engineer isn't disappearing. The job is evolving.

I think a lot of the anxiety around AI comes from imagining that software engineering is just turning requirements into lines of code. If that were true, AI really would be a massive threat to the profession.

But the job has always been more than that. We understand problems, make decisions, negotiate requirements and work with stakeholders. We learn how systems fit together, investigate failures, make trade-offs, think about security, and maintain software long after the original developer has moved on. Increasingly, we'll do all of that with AI as another tool.

Perhaps the engineer of the future writes less code by hand but understands more of the system. Perhaps they spend less time searching Stack Overflow and more time reviewing AI-generated solutions, or manage AI agents the way today's technical leads manage teams of developers. Perhaps the most valuable skill will be knowing enough to recognise a good implementation when you see one, even if you didn't write it.

I don't know exactly where that leads, and I don't think anyone does yet. But I do know I don't want an AI making decisions about a system simply because nobody was around to question it.

## The combination I want

I don't want a future where AI disappears into the background and does everything for us. I don't want one where engineers refuse to use it because they're worried about their jobs either. I'd rather see the two working together.

Give me an AI that can explore solutions very quickly, generate code, analyse problems and take care of repetitive work. Then give me an engineer who understands the system, the business and the risks, and isn't afraid to look at the AI's answer and say, *"No, that's not right."*

The AI brings speed, scale and the ability to explore more possibilities than one person could alone. The engineer brings context, experience, judgement and accountability. As AI gets better at producing convincing answers, that second half becomes more important, because someone still has to decide whether those answers deserve to be trusted.

The engineers who get the most from AI will be the ones who treat it as a way to become better engineers, and who stay capable of reviewing everything it produces.
